blocks.x: I look like a gentleman.
Let me give your names to bourgeois. How do you pronounce your name?
Joseph Bourgeois.
And I might give the spelling here too because-
B-O-U-R-G-E-A-U. A-U. G-O-S-E-P-H.
Because I've known people that had the same name spelled a little bit different too. Like O-I-S something on the end. And your real name is Joseph but they call you Fan.
They call me Fan for short, nickname.
You said because you looked like you were Chinese?

I looked like a Chinaman, that's why they call me that. And we started, I started around 29. No, I started before 29 playing with different little bands. And I first started playing with a plectum banjo. Was that five strings? Five strings, plectum banjo. Then I left it go and I began to play piano a little.
Can you tell me just where you were born? Is it here in the city?
I was born 1933, Orleans Street, New Orleans, Louisiana.
What was the date, remember the exact date?
Can you remember about the earliest music you ever heard? Was there any music around your home that your folks played?

Oh yeah, no of my folks never played but there's a lot of fellas like Paul Dominguez. Was he playing violin? Violin, he was playing in them days. And Piron, he was playing in those days. And I just can't call a lot of those guys names, you know what I mean? I forgot a lot of them. Oh sure. And Chris Kelly, Kid Rainey, Frankie Duesen, a lot of those guys, you know what I mean? And oh there's so many of them. And Freddie Washington, well I'm- Oh the piano player. He was the piano player, you know him.
He's very sick now in California. Yeah, yeah. And I saw him last year.
And Lewis, well a lot of the boys are dead that I know played. There's a gang of them that died. One guy died just last week here, what's his name? Simeon.
Oh Simeon, yes.
Simeon, Simeon, that's right.
The clarinet player.

That's right, he died in New York, somewhere up the line there. Yes. And I played with Kid Rainey lots of times. And we had a little band of our own. We had Pico was playing with us, Albert Francis, Pete Alexander, and myself. And we just had a little folk concert. And then I played for Frank Quintella when he had a place at Toulouse in Decatur. We played there for about two years. We had a little band, you know, playing around. And we played in a lot of little places. We even played at the ballet club, right in the front bar. George and I played there with a Vanscritticus drummer. I don't know whether you all know him or not.
No, what's his name? Do you remember?
I just can't call his name.
He's been taught.

Yeah, he used to, you know, introduce the people as they come in. Yes, so and so and so and so and so and so and so. And they wouldn't know him. My good friend and we'd get to playing and all that kind of stuff, you know what I mean? And we'd play at that Oaks place out there on the Airline Highway in the 4900s.
Wait a minute, was that you and George Gayno, you say?

What? Playing at the ballet? Yeah, me and George Gayno was a drummer. I was playing the piano. George was playing a ton of guitar and this fellow was playing the drum. And he was interlocking, you know what I mean? Full of talking his throat. Yeah. I just couldn't make out, you know. And then every time somebody would come in, well then he'd say something about him and, you know, make the crowd laugh and all that kind of stuff. And that's how we played there most, you know, until we, until they, after the song I know the place burned down I believe. And they had to repair it and we never worked there before. And who else, well we played, I played with so many different opinions. I played with Kid Thomas over the river. I didn't play with George Lewis. I played with this fellow here plays the cornet around here. What's his name? Howard? Howard. Not the boys on St. Philip Street.
Kid Howard.
Kid Howard. I played with Kid Howard and Ernest Milton and what is...
Ernest Milton, what does he play? A drum.
He's a drummer.
Is he still around? Yeah, he's around. I guess maybe I know if I see him. I don't remember the name.
Yeah, while we're here we should take notes on some of these fellas fans, you know, so many fellas around here that we never hear of.
Well, I know a gang of them.
Well I was going to ask a little bit more about your life. How old were you when you first took up music?
Well I started to play when I was around. Johnnie Simpson was the one who taught me how to play the guitar. Well he started. When I got away from it, you see what I mean? I was around nine years old.
Did you say your first instrument then was guitar or the plectum banjo?

Well I mean I first started playing the guitar. Then a fellow by the name of Wallace gave me one of those old plectum banjos and I began to learn. The fellas come and got me to play and I said well this is sort of a good racket. So I bought me a banjo and I played it and played it and played it and you know, stopped and played it over again and I began to start taking the piano then. See I belonged to a club, they bought a brand new pan and I was a member of the club and all I do is sit down and practice.
What club was that?

That was the Orleans Pleasure Club. That's where I first met Jellarole Morton. Oh he was around then? He was around. Jellarole Morton used to come play for us every Monday. We used to cook bean dinners for him. He would come play sometimes, cook a cow and dinner for him or so like that you know and he would come on. And then when I was in Chicago I met a fellow by the name of Manny Jones. I don't know if you know Manny Jones.
Oh yes, Richard M. Jones, yeah I knew him.
And then when I was in Chicago and I met Oliver and I met Frederick Kepard and I met a gang of them. When did you go to Chicago? In 22. Did you stay long? I stayed 60 days, that's all.
Did you work much as a musician or just not too busy?

No I was just you know on a vacation like, on a pleasure trip like, you see what I mean? So I went to Chicago and stayed there 60 days and I come on back home and went back to work. I didn't play no music you know. Well we had a piano where we were living and that's why I met Manny Jones. Oh yes. And he says what you gonna do, you gonna stay around Chicago? I says no I'm going back home. I'm going back home to go to work.
What trade did you follow by the way?
Well I was a lotter vendor.
Oh.
I worked at Lacha for 36 years about. You see now I'm on a pension and everything's over now. Of course I get jobs, little jobs you know what I mean.
So you're over 65 now is that right? Yeah I'm 68.
Yeah that's right. I'm on 1891, I'm 68. I'm 68 July the 29th past. And that's my old banjo up there now.
What? Up there on the, oh yeah. Yeah, nice looking banjo.
I got that's a, that's an epiphone.
What was an epiphone?
Mmhmm. Got a real nice tune to it too.
When did, when did you play a jumper that lasts, Fran? Huh? When did you play a jumper that lasts? About three cents a ago.

Three cents a ago? Mmhmm. Where? On a picnic. Oh yeah. Still, still working. Oh yeah, yeah. Well we played on that too. You know I got a friend of mine, you know, Riley. You know Riley, don't you? You mean Riley? Oh yeah. Well you see sometimes he gets a little miffed up and he sends me on his job at, well in fact it was my job. Yeah. I hired all the fellas in the turn around cause I used to let me slide. Yeah. And she fired me. But now when Riley wants to lay off, well then I go and play in his place until he gets back, you know what I mean? And cause I used to play there when Big Al Lewis was playing there. Him and I was playing there together. Walter Deku, I don't know if you know them guys. Yes.
By the way, you know where Walter Deku is? Have you seen him lately?
No, I don't know where he's at. He had been up in… He's around Baconda Street somewhere.
Well, around Tom Alberts there next door. I don't think he's there now, somebody told me. I'm not sure, I have to check with Tom and Mark.
Now there's, now I don't know if you know this guy, he's, what is this boy's name? His name is Paul Anderson. I think his name is Paul Anderson. He's a songster.
No, I don't think I know him.

No, you don't know. He used to sing in the alley with, that guy is going away now. He's, he was a cornet player. All those guys are going now. I don't know where they at, but they all, they all gone away. And we used to, I used to play with, oh there's so many of them guys. I just can't call all their names.
We'll ask some more about those. I was going to ask about the, when you were a boy again, you say there wasn't much music in your home, the rest of the family. No, no music in my home.
Can you remember the type of bands you heard?
When you were even five or six years old, can you remember back that far? Sure. What kind of bands they had?

Well they had the Maple Leaf Rag band, the Maple Leaf band. And they had, when I was a youngster, well then, Freddie Kepard, I was living right next door to Freddie's house in the way of speaking, because my aunt used to live there and I used to hear him play all the time, you know what I mean? He was playing the violin at first. And I used to hear him playing, his brother was a guitar player.
Yes, I know him very well. Louis.

Well then, by then playing and then we had a little, we used to play just a guitar, just the two guitars and go out and play little jobs and all that kind of stuff. Were you and Louis? No, me and a boy by the name of Fredolution. I was talking to him yesterday, there's another boy. He's around. Oh yeah, he's around.
Fred knows a lot of these boys and we never hear.

I just forgot a lot of them. Fredolution? Fredolution, now he's a blues singer. That's what he is, he's a blues singer, he's a good blues singer too. I was at his place yesterday and I said, we've got to get together and I want to take you to a friend of mine's house and I said, we're going to go there one day and just sit down and play a couple of numbers, you know what I mean? I just want him to hear you sing the blues. And this other boy, Paul, well he's a sentimental singer, he's a good singer too. Oh there's a lot of fellas around here that play and sing. Where does that he live, this Freddie Lucius? I don't know where he lives but he's a, he's a bobertender at St. Peter in Durginville. You know what I said? St. Peter? Yeah, I remember. That's where he's at. I was there yesterday and the man, you see the man you bought the bass from? Yes. Well then, he's going away. He bought his house and he's going back to pull off to Texas and he's going to, by the way he says, he said, man I got a bass in the back that I'd like to get rid of. I said, well come on, I'll take it to a man right now if you want to go. So we went up there and he wasn't there. Oh you were there too. Yeah.
I was in back but they didn't, there was a sign, ring bell. I was back in back.
Well I know, I said, well what's the use of me ringing the bell? He ain't there. You know what I mean?
I start two, three times to ring the bell.
Because I went over, we passed, you know.
The grocery store said they thought I wasn't in.
They told you. Yeah, they told me that when I seen the sign I said, oh well, he's not there, tend to use me ringing the bell.
Anyway, we got the bass.
Say Frank, what I'd like to ask you while we're here, you were talking with Minetta one time with Fess there and you were talking about the early days in the district when you were just real young.
Oh yeah, well I had an uncle that was, he, my uncle lived in the district all his life and whenever I wanted some money I'd go to him and get it. See the man?
And you remember such as Fess playing. Who was that? You remember Fess Minetta, you remember him?
Oh yeah, I met Fess a long time. I mean, Minetta, I met him oh years ago. And in them days they were getting but a dollar a night.
Do you remember when Minetta was playing the Lulus?

Yeah, yeah, 335 Lululwights, yeah. I know Lululwights like I know you. I know her better than I know you all because I've seen more of her, you know what I mean? Oh yeah. Than I've seen, I even had her wig in my hand. She wore a wig? She wore a blonde wig. I didn't know that. I didn't know that, no.
We never knew her of course at all, but we read about her.
Yeah, well that's, that's, she was a great big sort of a dark brown skinned woman.
Why did she wear a wig, huh?
Well, she wanted good hair.
But she had her own hair too.
She had her own hair but she wanted good hair, you see what I mean?
She wore a wig. Oh, I see that.
Yeah, and now let me see, I'm trying to think of somebody else that.

But she, you mentioned, talking about Lula again, since you say you knew her, well I never knew her at all. She was, you say brown skinned, I thought she was very light. No she wasn't. It was the Octaroom, wasn't she? No she wasn't. She wasn't that light. No. The girls were lighter. Oh yeah, all the girls were lighter. They were lighter.

I thought Lula was that light too. No, she wasn't. You didn't know. Not the Lula I seen. Yeah. You know what I mean? But she had the blonde hair. She had a blonde wig and I had about that long. I didn't know I had hair. 15 inches long. Well what was the natural color of her hair? I don't know. Well you know, if you have bad hair, well you know it's the same color as anybody that's got that hair, you know? I see. And my uncle just lived right around the corner from Lula Weiss and he was a bottle man. Was what? He was a bottle man, you know? He'd go around the street and pick up bottles and everything. Oh. And he was a man that made, you know, fixed those fishing poles and everything. Oh yeah. You know the fishing poles that put that thing around them and he used to do that for all them guys and like I said Chief Rye and all them big guys you know, and then they'd go out to the lake with him and catch bait, you know, be with him and everything. Yeah. And that's how he made his living. But he was a professional gambler too, behind it, you know what I mean? And that's how he made his money.
So you planned, not to cut your album out there, do you remember those bands that played in the dance halls in those days? In the district?

Well, Paul Dominguez played and I can't call this man's name. He played. Oh, I can't, he was a violin player. In them days lots of guys was playing violin. Can't call that gentleman's name to say my life. Piron was one. Piron played in the district many times and this fellow played and…
Did they have a big band this fellow you're thinking of? No, they didn't have a big band.
They only had about four or five pieces.
Oh, I see.

Like all the string band? Well, they had violin. You see violin was carrying the lead all the time. Yeah. You see what I mean? Like Piron, Paul Dominguez, and this guy, what I'm trying to think of, I can't call his name.
Was it me, Valto?
That's it, Valto. Oh.
I knew he played with Joe Oliver in different lines at the time. That's the man.

He looked like an Indian fellow. He had straight black hair and he played the violin. That was Valto. He lived on St. Peter and Praia, them days. That's a long time. And who else? Well they used to have, you know they used to have pianos in all those places, you know? Oh yeah. About those. That fellow's a lot. We used to play for, what's that woman's name? Ida Jackson. Oh yeah. I played a many jobs there.
Ida Jackson, did she have a house? Did she have one of the language ladies?
Yeah, she had a house and we used to play there. And our piano player was, his name was Herbert Bloom. He's in California right now. Good piano player.
I didn't know him, no.
No. Not the Bloom? Bloom, Herbert Bloom. Herbert Bloom. He was a good piano player.
Who else was in your band then that I didn't answer?
Oh, well Ida Jackson used to play with us too, Burbank. You know, Burbank.
Or Albert Burbank. Albert Burbank, yeah.

Well when he was, you know, didn't have a regular job, but whenever I wanted a client to play and couldn't get Pico, I'd get him. And then sometime I'd get this fellow, George, George Thomas, that's cornbread. Oh yeah, yeah. Brother Conrad. Brother Conrad, yeah. I'd get him. I'd get him to play and he'd play when we'd have a job or so. You know this fellow, Ida? Willie Jackson?
No, I never, a singer? Singer, yeah. New Orleans, they call it New Orleans Willie Jackson. Yeah, Willie Jackson.
He was singing at Tom Anderson's, right at Iberville and Ramport.
Did you ever work at Tom Anderson's too?

No, I never worked at Tom Anderson's, never did. Never did work at Tom Anderson's. But we used to see, when them times we used to go around and play, you know what I mean, for different people, you know. Yeah. And we used to go around and play just for fun, you know. I had the fellows that say, man let's go to my so and so's house today, you know. Pete would take his violin. I'd take my, I'd, sometime I'd take my banjo, sometime I'd tear the piano, I wouldn't take my banjo. I'd play the piano, you see what I mean?
Oh fine, now something you mentioned earlier, what year about would that be when you spoke about, you heard Jelly Roll more?
Oh that's been, that's before I went to the war, that's around 19, 1920, something like that.
Oh yeah, real early. What, you mean the First World War? Yeah. Or before the First World War?

Well yeah, yeah, I didn't go to war until I was 26. I was 26 years old when I came back. But Jelly Roll, you see, they had a fella, he was a, I'm talking about Fred's daddy, he was a good ball player, you see. Freddie Washington?
No, Freddie Lucian. Oh Freddie Lucian.
Daddy was a good ball player and in them days they had what you call a league club, you know, and this guy picked them up around 25, you ever know anything about 25?
Oh yes, I used to see it, I never got inside though.
Well, them guys used to be around there, you see, and this guy brought him around, this Freddie Lucian brought Jelly Roll more than to our club when we got the piano.
By the way, where was that Orleans club?
Orleans and Pritz, still there. Still there. But I mean it's not no club, no. It's a corner, let's see. It's right straight up this way.
It's on, I mean, is it towards uptown or downtown?
It's just like this corner right here, right there, you know? Across the street? Yeah, across the street on this side, you know, facing the riverside. On the riverside. That's right.
On the riverside and on the downtown.

Yeah, that's it. Take a picture of it that was downtown. Yeah, Orleans Pleasure Club, that was Orleans Pleasure Club. Did you put on parades too? No, I never did on parades. No, no, no, no, just parties. I never tried to make a second line in my life. Really? I never did. I never did. When the parades be coming, the parades be over there, I go over here. I never did like a second line on a parade, I don't know why. But they used to have them. Yes, and when I was in the PWA band, I don't know where they got so many of them. I don't know what to become of the picture. And I'm sitting right on the end, you know what I mean? They can distinguish me, you know, very, you know, because I was bright, a whole lot brighter than the other boys, you see what I mean? By me sitting on the end, I don't know what to become of the picture. And we all, we did, they had over 75 banjo players. And over 40 clarinets. I mean I had never seen a big ban, but we never did play nothing. You know what I mean? So I'm sitting in the band, you know what I mean? I was playing at the Pelican then, when Fate and Marvel and them was playing on the boat, on the steamer captain. And then the lottery closed, and I had to get due, and so the boss man gave me a job playing there. I said, get me a little band. And that's what I got, I got Poinnell. I learned Poinnell how to play piano.
Oh yeah, I had to Poinnell. I had to Poinnell.

I learned him how to play the piano, and I got Alvin Francis, and I got a boy by the name of Deli Hoosier to play saxophone, and I played the banjo. And we played there, and we was getting $37 a week. $37 a month. A month? And Sherry Wine was a nickel a trough, and a big glass like that, a nickel.
Sherry Wine?

Sherry Wine, Lange Liquor, Claret Wine, and all that kind of stuff. And then Fate and Marvel and them used to come, Tab Smith. You know Tab Smith? I remember. A saxophone player? I remember. Out of St. Louis? Well he'd come down. Well I know Tab because he used to buck every night.
Is he still around?

I don't know. Where is he at? So when Tab and them would come and play for us, well we'd all, you know, let them play. Instead of us playing. You see what I mean? He was on the boat then. He was on the boat playing with Fate and Marvel. And I had Bunnell playing piano with me. You see what I mean? So now and then we'd say, well, see Fate, he'd play high society for us. And Fate would play, you know, he's high society like he'd play. So when he'd get through playing I'd say, all right Bunnell. You know what I mean? I'd say, play high society for fate. You all never knew him, huh?
No, but I've heard about Lester told us a little bit.

Yes, indeed. He was the baddest piano player they had in the city in the Orleans. He was one of the best and couldn't really know. Fingers like Liv Rache. He could play just like Liv Rache in my book. You know what I mean? I'd say, just Albert and him play, I said, yeah I'm going to take me a little while Jack. Because I could never catch up with him. You know what I mean? His fingers was too fast. You understand? Because he'd play high society. Well he'd start to play in it. Then I'd say, all right, imitate Earl Hines. He'd imitate Earl Hines. I'd say, now, imitate Duke Ellington. He'd imitate Duke Ellington. I'd say, imitate Wayne King. He'd imitate Wayne King. You know any piano player that you could name, that he could play, he could imitate him. And see like sophisticated lady, all them car numbers, man he could play them numbers down. And nobody showed it to him. I don't know how he got them. I'm telling you. He had a wonderful ear. Oh he had this. And even, I know you know this guy too, his name is, he's got the music shop on there. He's got the music shop on Broad Street. Peter.
Peter. Peterson.
Peterson, yeah Peterson. Now we had a piano in Peterson's place on Claiborne Street when he had the piano. We used to go down and practice all the time.
Oh right in Peterson's place. Well where was the place on Claiborne Street?
On Claiborne between St. Peter and Lafitte.
Yeah, I never knew it then.
And he says, man I just wish I could have took them numbers down that he played. You know, record them. Well in them days I don't think they had a recording outfit. No, not like this.
No.

He couldn't get no, he couldn't have no recording outfit to pick up on them numbers. Yeah. And that's how we used to do too, you know what I mean? And he said, no I was talking to them there today and he said, man I wish I could have recorded them numbers. He said they weren't money. Let's see who else.
You never remember hearing such as Tony Jackson or any of those?

Yeah, Tony Jackson, yeah I know Tony Jackson well. Oh you know him well? Yeah, he used to be around there. What I've seen I used to have to go in the bar to get my uncle to give him some money. When I used to go in there and say, you know you don't belong in here. I said, oh well it's alright. I said, uncle I just want a couple of nickels you know. And when he gave it to him I go and buy my bill.
How was his playing, can you remember that?

Well he was a good piano player and a good singer too. Oh the same. Yeah, he was a good singer and a good piano player. Really good. Oh and there was so many of those guys around there. And Calvin Jackson and he was a piano player. Ed Moishier. I'm talking about the way back you know. And all them was fellas that hanged around the district you know what I mean. Couldn't play piano you know what I mean.
It's interesting that you hear those names. Remember Alfred Wilson?
Alfred Wilson? No, I don't know him.
There was another fella, Cahill, was his name? Carole or Carole?
Alvin Carole.
Carole. Alvin Cal.
How would you say that?
How would you pronounce it? How would you spell it? I've heard that name sometimes. Alvin Cal. Yeah.
He was a piano player. Would you say Cahill?
Something like that?
You know how to spell that?
It must be a Creole name. Yeah, well those Creole names are tough.
How would you spell that from?
I wouldn't know. Cal Cahill?

Cal Cahill? Cal, no it wouldn't be that. And there's another boy right down here who's a nice musician now. His name is uh, he played with us too. He's right there in the- What's that name again? Tontley Sallagier. Tontley Sallagier. Tontley Sallagier. What's that name again? Tontley Sallagier. Tony Sallagier. Sallagier. Sallagier. Sallagier. Sallagier. Yeah, he's living. He's still living? Yeah, he's right over there right now. He's working. Where in Seattle? No, he was a cornet player. A cornet player.
Yeah, no, no, no.
He was a cornet player. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. He's right over there right now. He's working. Playing in Seattle? No, he was a cornet player. A cornet? Yeah. He used to play with, he used to play around here with Fats and them too. Oh yeah? Yeah. And then when I'd get him to play, you know, and I'd get a quick up job, you know, I'd
still-
Fats, you call him. Fats Pichon, yeah. He's in Chicago now, yeah. Fats is in Chicago. That's-
Yes, he'd been up there at the absent house.

Yeah, ever since the absent house closed down and he's up there playing. Then his mother's up there too, you know. And I'm trying to think of some man, and I know so many guys, but I'm just like I was saying, like what's this guy's name? Moe. He's a clarinetist too, Moe. Noon, Noon, Noon, something like that. Not Noon, the business. The boy was playing the clarinetist and went to Chicago, Noon. It was Jimmy Noon. Jimmy Noon. Jimmy Noon. I knew him up there. He was one of the boys around there too. And all there's so many of them gone with and I forgot a lot of them. I forgot their names and everything, you know what I mean?
That you would remember such as Joe Oliver.

Yeah, I was in Chicago when Joe Oliver was in Chicago playing at the Dreamland Cabaret on the Dreamland Cabaret on the Dreamland Cabaret on the Dreamland Cabaret on the Dreamland Cabaret. And that's where I met this guy, Marnie Jones. That's where I met them in 22. Now that's a good little bit. That's a good bit. When I was up there, just like on vacation, you know what I mean?
You remember very well, remember all of these people.
And I know a lot of us, but I just can't think of their names.
Yeah, I know. It's tough to think of a college name.
And some of the boys around Chicago, but I mean New York, that's playing saxophone right now. Some of them now, you catch that Morgan boy that's playing with Cab Callaway.
With Al Morgan. Al Morgan played a bass player.

Well, he left here and went to Chicago. And, oh, there was so many other fellas, you know what I mean, that played and played around here and all that kind of stuff, you know what I mean? But I just, it's like, I forget them.
I was going to ask a little bit about when you started on piano, did you have, that's already going there. Did you have anybody to show you on piano, give you lessons or?
No, I just picked it up from the banjo, from the guitar on the banjo.
Now, on the banjo you said Johnny Sincere.
Well, Johnny Sincere on the guitar, yeah. First, you know, I got some lessons from him, because I liked it and I used to worry life out of him to show him some chords, you know what I mean?
I got a whole outfit there, no, no. Did that on the guitar?
I got a guitar, I got an amplifier, I got a recording outfit and everything right in there.
Did he teach you to read or just show you the chords?
No, he just showed me the chords, no. In other words, I was a sort of a catch-behind musician, you know?
Show me this, uh, sure, man.
He's a guitar player too. Oh, yeah, but I'm going to learn.
Is he in a Navy band a picture of a...
No, that's, he's in the Navy now.
Oh, he's not a band, that's the... No, that's, uh, he's in there, but you can't, all the... Yes. You don't know him and, uh, he's right here.
First off, that's going to be a big picture of a Navy band.
And I want to show you some of the... And, uh, Moran, you know Moran, Legend of Miles' brother. I got a picture of somewhere of the band and everything, but I can't find it.
Oh, yeah.
Well, we were playing together, you know, George and I, and Urban Moran, and Milton, and myself.
What a minute, Milton?
Milton, Ernest Milton.
